name: One-nation conservatism
summary: One-nation conservatism is the British paternalist strand of Toryism that defends established institutions such as the Crown and Church while holding that the privileged owe duties to the poor. It sees society as an organic, hierarchical whole that should be reconciled across classes through social reform and gradual change rather than class conflict or doctrinaire markets. In practice it accepted the post-war welfare state and mixed economy and is pragmatic rather than ideological.
scope: Disraelian Tory democracy (Coningsby, Sybil, the 1872 Crystal Palace speech) as carried on by Baldwin, Chamberlain, Butler and Macmillan in the post-war consensus and by later self-described one-nation Tories. Excludes the New Right and Thatcherite free-market strand, and non-British conservatisms. Several modern issues were never addressed and are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Rab Butler
keyFigures.role: Architect of the post-war 'new conservatism' and the Industrial Charter.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Post-war one-nation Conservatives accepted the NHS and welfare state as part of the consensus, treating basic provision as an obligation of a united society.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not a classic one-nation question; paternalists favour protecting workers, but pragmatic Tories worried about business costs and were split.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: One-nationers accepted markets and private enterprise but explicitly rejected the New Right claim that markets beat state action across the board; adherents are split.

public-ownership.rationale: The Industrial Charter accepted a mixed economy and consensus-era nationalisations but criticised Labour planning; one-nationers tolerated rather than advocated public ownership.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Noblesse oblige asks the privileged to share, mainly through duty and charity; whether this meant significantly higher taxes is not settled and varied by era.

unions-good.rationale: Disraeli's 1875 Acts protected collective action and the Industrial Charter pledged to safeguard workers' rights, so unions were seen as a legitimate partner in class reconciliation.

property-fundamental.rationale: Conservatives treat property as part of the inherited order, though one-nationers qualify it with duties to those below.

cut-welfare.rationale: One-nationism arose to give social support; the New Right's attack on welfare dependency is documented as the position it opposed.

worker-ownership.rationale: Class harmony within the existing order rather than transferring ownership to workers; the idea is socialist and not part of Tory paternalism.

surveillance-ok.rationale: No documented one-nation position; authority-minded conservatism leans yes while civil-liberties Tories dissent.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Never addressed; pragmatic Tories supported public-order laws but some prize free speech, so adherents are split.

strong-leader.rationale: One-nationism works through parliament, institutions and compromise, not leaders bypassing gridlock.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.

reviewHistory.rationale: Order, authority and the maintenance of institutions and empire lead conservatives to back the forces of the state.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

traditional-family.rationale: Conservatives see family, property and religion as foundations of social order.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Cameron-era one-nationers legalised it while older and religious Tories opposed; the strand is genuinely split.

abortion-legal.rationale: Traditionally a matter of conscience in the Conservative Party; one-nationers divided between religious caution and pragmatic reform.

more-religion-public.rationale: Disraeli defended the Church as an institution of the nation and conservatives see religion as a key tradition, though one-nationism is not theocratic.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Maintaining national institutions and traditions is the first of Disraeli's three great objects.

gradual-change.rationale: Society is seen as an organism that should develop naturally; reform is piecemeal and respects institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not a defining one-nation issue; Powellite restrictionists and pragmatic moderates both claim the Tory tradition.

free-trade.rationale: The Industrial Charter turned against protection while Disraeli backed an imperial tariff, so the tradition is split on free trade.

nation-first.rationale: Disraeli contrasted national and imperial greatness with cosmopolitan Liberalism, putting country first.

open-borders.rationale: A tradition of nation, institutions and patriotism rejects open borders as incompatible with national community.

revolution-justified.rationale: The movement was motivated by preventing revolution through reform, and conservatives oppose revolutionary change.

experts-over-public.rationale: Authority and hierarchy favour elite judgment, but Tory democracy courted the electorate; adherents are split.

central-planning.rationale: One-nation Tories accepted Keynesian management but criticised Labour's planning as producing bloat and restrictions.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Burke-derived conservatism ties liberty to inheritance, so heavy death duties are disliked.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Disraeli backed an imperial tariff while the Industrial Charter opposed protectionism; adherents were split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Interwar Chamberlain and Baldwin intervened while the Charter sought incentives over direction; no consensus.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Socialist abolition of wages contradicts class reconciliation within the existing order.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Pragmatic institutionalism and acceptance of Keynesian management oppose abolition.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Cooperation between employers and workers is valued, but formal state-recognised price-setting bodies are not a one-nation tenet.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Disraeli named maintaining the institutions of the country, especially the monarchy, as the first Tory object.

democracy-best.rationale: Tory democracy accepted the enlarged franchise, though hierarchy and doubts about majority rule temper enthusiasm.

direct-votes.rationale: Conservative preference for representative institutions over majoritarian plebiscites.

workers-councils.rationale: Socialist-derived structures rejected in favour of parliament and established institutions.

right-to-secede.rationale: Disraeli opposed disintegration of the empire; Unionist tradition values national unity.

natural-rulers.rationale: Disraeli viewed society as naturally hierarchical with those on top owing duties; the premise is accepted with obligation attached.

political-violence-never.rationale: Concerned with stability and order, though some force is accepted for state authority.

separate-church-state.rationale: Defended an established Church as national institution; strict separation is opposed.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Religion is valued as tradition but one-nationism is pragmatic, not theocratic.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Paternalist state obligations and institutional trust rule out privatised justice and defence.

ethnic-nation.rationale: One-nation means class unity within a nation, not ethnic homogeneity; Disraeli's empire was multi-ethnic.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Class reconciliation and mutual obligation reject class conflict as the engine of history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Hierarchy is accepted as natural; reducing hardship is not equalising outcomes.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Disraeli championed the empire; modern one-nationers are pragmatic but reject reparations.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Disraeli faulted Liberals as selfish individualists; the doctrine stresses mutual duty.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Mutual obligation and noblesse oblige are core; conservatism leans toward authority.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: No stated position; stewardship sentiment is present but not defining.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Sybil laments industrial inequality but seeks to reform, not repudiate, industrial society.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Opposed to disrupting existing institutions; change should be gradual.

restore-past-order.rationale: Disraeli romanticised the older order, but one-nationism accepts evolving adaptation rather than restoration.

results-over-ideology.rationale: One-nationism presents itself as pragmatic and non-ideological, judging policies by their effect on stability.

direct-action.rationale: Works through parliament and institutions; direct action is outside the tradition.

means-match-ends.rationale: Not a conservative formulation; change should be gradual yet no stated link of means and ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Contrary to organic, evolved, civilised society.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Hierarchy and ordered society reject the idea.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Safety-net provision exists but distribution by need as the general principle is socialist.

production-for-use.rationale: Accepts private enterprise and profit incentives.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Class reconciliation denies that profit is exploitation.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Empire is defended and the thesis is Marxist-Leninist.

taxation-theft.rationale: Paternalist state support requires taxation as legitimate.

harm-principle.rationale: Paternalism holds that the state promotes welfare and morality, not just prevents harm.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Conservatives stress duties, community and institutions rather than individual rights alone.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Tory democracy values political participation and rejects the exit logic of the New Right.

state-as-business.rationale: Mutual obligation and paternalism are distinct from commercial customer logic.

positive-liberty.rationale: Support for social reform and material support for the poor accords with this idea, though not framed in those terms.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not a one-nation claim; more a populist-right trope.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Race and ability are never discussed; the tradition's focus is class duty, and rejection is assumed.

organic-representation.rationale: Organic society appeals but representation is through parties in parliament in practice.

total-state.rationale: Opposes engineered society and totalising state; conservatism distrusts rational planning.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Disraeli championed imperial expansion, but modern one-nationers do not seek territory.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rule through parliamentary institutions, not feudal oaths, though Disraeli romanticised the feudal ideal.

bound-labor.rationale: Disraeli sympathised with the poor and opposed the poor's degradation.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Particularist scepticism but not relativism about truth.

universal-morality.rationale: Conservatives vary; Burkean particularism sits against religious natural-law belief.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Class cooperation, not worker control, is the aim.

school-vouchers.rationale: The New Right's market mechanism is not one-nation, though Butler's reforms preserved a mix.

economic-freedom.rationale: One-nationers accept markets but not the New Right claim that political liberty depends on them.

rule-by-example.rationale: Noblesse oblige holds elites must lead by honourable example, though laws still apply.

national-self-determination.rationale: Not a stated tenet; Disraeli prioritised empire over self-determination.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Conservatism distrusts unchecked reason and values religion and tradition.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Butler's updated conservatism stressed self-reliance and aid for those in need, while Disraeli's tradition resisted harsh poor-law conditions.

class-collaboration.rationale: Reconciling employers and workers rather than letting them become opposed nations is the founding idea.

workers-nation.rationale: The working class is meant to be integrated into the nation rather than organised internationally.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Hierarchy supports traditional roles in older sources, modern one-nationers reject legal distinction.

ban-interest.rationale: Usury law is never discussed; rejection is assumed because the tradition accepts a market economy.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Segregation law is never discussed; rejection is assumed from the one-nation theme of social unity.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Denies the Marxist view and sees the state as serving all classes.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: National tradition favours integration but is not clearly stated; adherents divided.

proportional-representation.rationale: Tories, as defenders of the constitution, preferred first-past-the-post.

national-mission.rationale: Disraeli emphasised imperial moral greatness, but modern one-nationers do not export government.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Conservatism tends to deny systematic male advantage as structural oppression.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The tradition is built on a responsible governing elite.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics is never discussed; rejection is assumed from the tradition's humanitarian social reformism.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Directly opposed to the paternalist state and social protection.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Mixed marriage is never discussed; rejection is assumed from the tradition's theme of national unity across classes.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Disraeli's concern for the poor and common humanity underlies the reforms, though hierarchy is accepted.

socialism-one-country.rationale: This Marxist debate is never discussed by one-nation conservatives; disagreement is assumed from their anti-socialism.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Disraeli championed the empire and settler colonies.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Cow protection is never discussed; rejection is assumed because it has no place in British Tory politics.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Religion is seen as a key tradition.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: This Marxist-Leninist doctrine is never discussed; disagreement is assumed from the tradition's rejection of socialism.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Tory democracy accepted mass franchise as legitimating government.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Disraeli attacked morbid competition (Sybil) and sought cooperation.

vanguard-party.rationale: Marxist-Leninist doctrine opposite to this tradition.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Concern for the condition of the people is one of the three objects.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Thatcher-era policy opposed by some one-nationers; split.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Disraeli's 1875 Acts protected peaceful picketing while later Conservative governments restricted strikes, so the tradition is divided.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Disraeli blamed social institutions and inequality.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Not a one-nation claim; Disraeli's imperial vision multi-ethnic.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Sortition is never discussed; rejection is assumed from the tradition's belief in a responsible governing elite.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Wartime acceptance, but not a tenet.

party-commands-army.rationale: Incompatible with constitutional monarchy and parliament.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: MPs' pay is never discussed; rejection is assumed from the tradition's acceptance of a governing elite.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Constitutional monarchy has ministers responsible to parliament.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Supports the established episcopal Church of England.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Imperial and national power orientation favours alliances.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Disraeli romanticised the old rural order.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Disraeli held imperial England had higher national character.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Never addressed in the sources; traditionalists object while pragmatic modernisers accept it, so adherents split.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conservatives value custom and conformity to tradition.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not a stated view; Disraeli stressed political and imperial ties, with no claim that independence requires remaking property.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Never addressed in the sources; national attachment to territory is offset by pragmatic compromise.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Property carries duties to others per the noblesse oblige principle.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Divine kingship is never discussed; rejection is assumed because the British constitutional monarchy makes no such claim.

decide-locally.rationale: Organic society values local institutions, but Tory paternalism and the national Crown and parliament favour central action; no stated position.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The state is expected to use authority for order and empire; an absolutist non-aggression rule is a libertarian doctrine.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Tory defence of the Crown, Parliament and established institutions rests on constitutional, law-bound rule, so rulers are not above the law.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Disraeli defended the balance of Crown, Lords and Commons and an aristocracy leading a broad popular franchise, the classic mixed constitution.

leader-cult.rationale: Conservatives honour the Crown and institutions rather than party leaders, and treat prime ministers as officeholders; mass leader worship is foreign to the tradition.

equal-parenting.rationale: Never addressed; paternalist family conservatism and fairness to fathers pull in different directions, so adherents are split.

land-redistribution.rationale: Conservatism defends property and gradual change, and one-nation Tories sought reform of conditions, not seizing estates.

ban-cartels.rationale: Pragmatic mixed-economy Tories accepted some regulation, but there is no documented stance on cartels.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Parliamentary sovereignty and respect for established institutions pull in opposite directions; adherents are split.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Conservatism favours gradual change within institutions and rejects revolutionary action.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Disraeli and his successors defended the Crown and the established institutions of rank, and one-nation Tories resisted abolishing hereditary seats, though Macmillan's 1958 Act added life peers.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Disraeli's Toryism treats the nation as an organic historical whole and defends inherited institutions, so national history belongs at the centre of teaching.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Disraeli's Crystal Palace speech defended the Empire, and imperial paternalism was common among Tories; the statement is dated and later one-nation Tories largely dropped it.

patriotic-education.rationale: One-nation conservatism stresses national loyalty and shared institutions such as Crown and Church as the bond across classes.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The Industrial Charter and post-war consensus held that a regulated mixed economy could reconcile capitalism with social cohesion without collapse.

delink-world-market.rationale: One-nation Tories backed trade and the mixed economy within the existing order, and the idea of breaking economic ties contradicts their gradualism.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: The claim rests on Marxist class analysis, which one-nation conservatism rejects in favour of class reconciliation under mutual duties.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Burkean parliamentary sovereignty and distrust of abstract rights make one-nation conservatives resist entrenched written constraints.

elective-rulers.rationale: Disraeli defended the hereditary Crown and Lords as Tory institutions, so rulers are not to be chosen by election.

minority-veto.rationale: A minority veto contradicts the organic, pragmatic view of national government under parliamentary majorities; unanimity is not a Tory principle.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Tories honour the constitution and the Glorious Revolution settlement, but one-nation conservatism is gradualist and stresses order over resistance, so adherents are split.

parliament-supreme.rationale: One-nation Toryism defended the Crown in Parliament but accepted that Parliament governs in practice, as in Disraeli's constitutional monarchy.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Noblesse oblige and the duties of the privileged to the poor are the defining one-nation principle, as in Disraeli's Sybil.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Tory democracy and paternalism hold that the governing class has a duty to take part in public service.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A Marxist-style claim that one-nation Tories would not endorse; they value the national culture and its institutions as unifying, not as pacifying.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Conservatives hold that institutions win consent through habit and deference, but the strand would not frame this as ruling-class domination; adherents are split.

native-born-offices.rationale: Tories favour national belonging but the strand was pragmatic and the Crown and civil service were open to naturalised citizens; adherents are split.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Post-war one-nation Tories fought fascism, but treating it as constitutional founding doctrine is not a British Tory idea; adherents are split.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Disraeli's imperial protection and the Industrial Charter's opposition to protectionism point both ways; pragmatic and split.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Conservatism holds that representatives exercise judgement for the nation and are not mandated delegates; recall cuts against settled institutions.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: One-nation Conservatives accepted the post-war welfare state, so replacing state pensions with private accounts runs against the consensus.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Conservatism defends property and its social duties as established institutions, rejecting community ownership of land.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Parliament and the constitution are the institutions Tory democracy defends, and approval of supply by the Commons is settled practice.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: No documented stance; Tories defended property but the sources do not touch foreign ownership.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Never addressed; sovereignty-minded Tories and liberal one-nation Tories differ.

job-guarantee.rationale: The Industrial Charter accepted high employment as an aim but not a state guarantee of work as employer of last resort.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Burkean conservatism holds that order and respect for established law are owed as a matter of duty.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage is a traditional institution that Tory conservatism defends.

informal-organisation.rationale: One-nation conservatism trusts established institutions such as parties and Parliament over informal action.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The Industrial Charter accepted a mixed economy and Conservatives defend private property, so common ownership of the means of production is rejected.

religion-illusion.rationale: One-nation conservatism defends the established Church and religion as a social foundation and rejects the materialist view.

cooperative-communities.rationale: One-nation conservatism defends hierarchical, organic society and private property against communal reorganisation.

suppress-opposition.rationale: One-nation conservatism upholds parliamentary and constitutional institutions and orderly reform, not suppression.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Disraeli defended empire and an imperial tariff but also called for colonial self-government; mixed on this wording.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The strand holds to gradualism and order, so forcible removal of rulers is rejected.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Organic, hierarchical society with reform led by established elites; Tory democracy was paternalist rather than participatory.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: One-nation Tories are split on this modern question and the doctrine does not address it.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Pragmatic reconciliation of classes sounds like combining left and right ideas, but the strand also defends a lasting conservative tradition.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept; the strand rejects class conflict and Marxist analysis, but supports workers' welfare.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Crown and Church are central, yet the strand accepts parliamentary sovereignty; adherents are split.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Paternalism and protection of workers' rights as in the Industrial Charter point this way, though business costs worried pragmatic Tories.

social-market-economy.rationale: The Industrial Charter accepted a mixed economy with workers' rights while opposing Labour planning and protectionism, matching markets with social protection.

rich-first.rationale: Paternalists oppose a divided 'two nations' but also accept hierarchy and inequality; mixed.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a constitutional or ceremonial crown, and the statement now asks only about passing real governing power to a child.

reviewHistory.rationale: One-nation Tories defend the Crown and other inherited institutions as part of the organic social order, so hereditary succession in a monarchy is accepted.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a constitutional or ceremonial crown, and the statement now asks only about passing real governing power to a child.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

property-franchise.rationale: Disraeli's Tory democracy sought to bring working men into the constitution, as in the 1867 Reform Act, and the Crystal Palace speech addressed the people as a whole.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Conservatism in the Burkean tradition values established law and settled constitutional forms over arbitrary rule.

racial-franchise.rationale: The one-nation idea is that the whole nation is united across classes, which is incompatible with confining the franchise to one ethnic group.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: One-nation conservatism defends established institutions, notably the Church, so state atheism is the opposite.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: It prizes order and established institutions and was pragmatic, not abolitionist.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Disraeli stressed the privileged's duties but the strand accepted the welfare state; adherents split between voluntary and state help.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The strand defends the Church of England, which has divided over women's ministry; adherents split.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Industrial Charter and paternalist duties accept profit and property, so this is split.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Disraeli's Tory democracy sought to unite classes, not to reserve economic life for a majority group.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: One-nation Tories defend a hierarchical, organic society and rejected class rule, so they would not make working-class political power a condition of legitimacy; Disraeli sought class reconciliation instead.

municipal-property.rationale: Disraelian Toryism defends private property and rejected municipal or collective ownership of production; the Industrial Charter accepted only limited nationalisation.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Never addressed and adherents are split between pragmatic support for science and traditional caution about human nature.

online-anonymity.rationale: Never addressed; adherents split between pragmatic civil-liberty instincts and a preference for order and accountability.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The one-nation tradition defends the Church and Crown and treats society as having moral and spiritual dimensions, as Disraeli's Sybil and the Stanford entry on conservatism describe.

racial-group-interests.rationale: One-nation conservatism stresses a single national community across classes and rejects politics organised around group interests.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Disraeli's 1872 speech defended empire and a strong national defence, so a pure defensive-only rule does not fit the tradition.

future-generations.rationale: Conservative thought sees society as a partnership across generations, so handing on the inheritance undamaged follows from its organic view.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The Industrial Charter and the post-war consensus accepted strong trade unions and negotiated pay, though not as a principle of Disraeli's own.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Pragmatic one-nation Tories followed circumstance and Keynesian management, so binding fiscal rules are neither required nor rejected.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Disraeli's imperial paternalism and later aid policies point both ways, and the issue was not central to the strand.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Conservatism defends and reforms inherited institutions gradually; one-nation Tories would take over and use the state, never smash it.

internal-colonialism.rationale: One-nation Toryism stresses one nation against division, and regional exploitation as colonialism is outside its framework.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Conservatism is sceptical of redesigning society and human nature, and treats human nature as a fixed ground for institutions.

workers-own-party.rationale: Disraeli's Sybil and the Industrial Charter sought to reconcile classes within broad parties, not to build class-based parties.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Never addressed; pragmatic one-nation conservatives favoured firm order but also trust in judges as an established institution.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: The Industrial Charter accepted workers' rights but the strand never settled compulsory membership.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Tory democracy accepted elections as a means of reconciling classes, but its organic view of society goes beyond procedure; adherents are split.

national-church-status.rationale: One-nation conservatism defends established institutions including the Church of England as an object of Tory loyalty.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The strand accepted the post-war welfare state and mixed economy, which was universal rather than means-tested.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: It defends established institutions such as parties, Parliament, Crown and Church as part of the organic social order, not as obstacles.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: It defends the established Church and the Crown and treats religious institutions as part of the constitution.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Disraeli's national principle and his concern for the condition of the people link patriotism with serving the working poor, as in his Crystal Palace speech and Sybil.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: One-nation conservatism rejected state planning and one-party socialism, and the question presupposes communist rule that the strand opposed.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: One-nationism arose to give social support; the New Right's attack on welfare dependency is documented as the position it opposed. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: The wealthy and privileged have a duty to look after those less fortunate.
missingStatements.rationale: Noblesse oblige and mutual obligation between ranks are the defining one-nation principle.

missingStatements.text: Conservative parties should adopt social reforms to prevent a country dividing into a rich nation and a poor nation.
missingStatements.rationale: Disraeli's 'two nations' warning, and his view that neglect of popular suffering risks instability, is the founding argument.

missingStatements.text: The empire or overseas dominions of one's country are a source of national greatness worth maintaining.
missingStatements.rationale: Disraeli's Crystal Palace speech made upholding the empire a great Tory object.
missingStatements.declined: Historic imperial pride is dated and mostly captured by national-mission and territorial-expansion; not a live question.

notes: The strand is pragmatic and non-ideological, so many answers on modern issues are inferred. Disraeli's own era favoured protection and imperial tariffs while the post-war Charter opposed protectionism; Heath-era one-nationers were pro-European and later ones divided. Sources s2 and s3 were opened only in part.
